newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian parliament says stolen WW2 art should stay.
newsitem.headline: Russian parliament says stolen WW2 art should stay.

text.p: Russia's Federation Council, the upper house of parliament, overruled a presidential veto on Wednesday and passed a bill asserting Moscow's ownership to art treasures seized from Germany at the end of World War Two.
The results of a postal ballot on the issue showed that 144 deputies in the upper house had voted to confirm the bill, well above the 119 needed to overrule a veto.

President Boris Yeltsin must sign the bill into law in the next seven days, or challenge it in the Constitutional Court. His spokesman, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, told Interfax news agency Yeltsin would "not leave the decision without a reaction".

Declining to say how he would react but restating Yeltsin's view that the bill broke international law, Yastrzhembsky noted that the Kremlin had already said he might go to the Constitutional Court. He added that this was not the only possible response.
Germany expressed its disappointment with the vote and urged Yeltsin to try and block the law in court.
"The German government took notice of the Federation Council decision with regret," said a statement distributed by the German embassy in Moscow.

"The German government expects president Yeltsin to ask the Russian Constitutional Court to investigate the matter as he promised to German Chancellor Helmut Kohl when the two met in Baden-Baden on April 18."
Yeltsin's representative in the Federation Council, Alexander Kotenkov, said the chances were better than even that Yeltsin would appeal to the court.
"I expect the possibility of such a decision by the head of the state is more than 50 percent, but the final decision is up to the president," Interfax news agency quoted Kotenkov as saying.
The art, including a priceless Gutenberg bible and paintings by impressionists Claude Monet and Henri Matisse, was seized by the Soviet Red Army from museums and private homes in Germany.
Germany, Russia's biggest Western trading partner, wants the masterpieces back.
But many Russians argue they should stay in Russia as compensation for Soviet sufferings during World War Two. About 27 million Soviet citizens were killed in the war.

The Federation Council members who voted against overruling Yeltsin's veto said this step could have much wider negative impact on Russia then just Germany's displeasure with Moscow's reluctance to return the art.
"We need such a law but some of its articles contradict international agreements Russia has signed," Konstantin Titov, governor of the Samara region, told reporters after the voting.
Interfax quoted Deputy Culture Minister Mikhail Shvydkoi as saying the law would harm Moscow's image as a democracy and damage its relations with Western countries.
"This law may bring more harm than benefits," he said.
Mentimer Shaimiyev, president of the ethnic republic of Tatarstan, commented that Russians who have painful memories of the war could hardly have an unbiased judgement on the problem.
"We should have left the law to the next generation," he said. "Council members are themselves closing the door for Russia to develop in a normal and democratic way."
